summary: James Miller is a scholar in sinology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Cambridge (M.A. 1997) and Boston University (Ph.D. 2000), and served as Professor of Chinese Studies and Religious Studies at Queen's University Belfast (attested 2014).

James Morison was an Indologist who studied at the University of Oxford and the University of Vienna (Ph.D. c. 1889-1893) under Georg Bühler and Arthur Anthony Macdonell. In 1914, he served as Librarian at the Indian Institute, Oxford.

James Murdoch worked in Japanology and history/archaeology. After studying at the University of Aberdeen and under Theodor Benfey, he held posts at Kanazawa University (c. 1891-1893), the University of Tokyo (c. 1898-1900), and Kagoshima University (c. 1901-1908).

James Prinsep was an Indologist and historian/archaeologist. He served as Assay-Master at the Benares Mint (1820-1830) and Kolkata Mint (1830-1838), led The Asiatic Society (1832-1838), and founded the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal and Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum.

James Rennell was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served in the Bengal Engineers (1764) and as surveyor of Bengal holdings for the East India Company (1764-1777), later founding the Royal Geographical Society in 1830.

James Robert Ballantyne worked in Indology, philosophy, and linguistics. Educated at the East India Company College, Edinburgh, and Glasgow, he served as Principal of Sampurnanand Sanskrit University/Benares Sanskrit College (1845-1861) and later as Librarian at the India Office.

James Robson is a scholar of Buddhist studies, sinology, and religious studies. He earned his BA at UC Santa Barbara and PhD at Stanford. He held posts at Michigan and Harvard, where he became Harvard-Yenching Institute Director in 2024.

James Roland Ware was an Indologist, sinologist, and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Pennsylvania and under Franklin Edgerton and Sylvain Lévi. He held posts at Lehigh, University of Washington, Harvard-Yenching Institute, and Harvard University (1932-1934).

James Smith Reid was a historian and archaeologist who studied at the University of Cambridge (c. 1865-1869). He held academic posts at Christ's College (1869-1880), Pembroke College (1873-1885), and Gonville and Caius College (1878-1926).

James Stark was an active figure in Indology and history/archaeology. He served as Puisne Justice on the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka in 1840 and as President of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka in 1845.

James Stewart King was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He completed his education at Trinity College Dublin and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst (c. 1867-1868).

James Sutherland Cotton worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. Educated at Winchester College and Trinity College, Oxford (1867-1870), he served as a Fellow and Lecturer at Queen's College, Benares, and at Queens' College between 1871 and 1874.

James Taft Hatfield was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. Educated at Northwestern (A.B., A.M.) and Johns Hopkins (Ph.D.), he taught at Rust College (1884-1885) and served as a professor at Northwestern University from 1890 to 1934.

James Talboys Wheeler worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as Professor of Moral and Mental Philosophy at Presidency College, Chennai (c. 1858-1862) and as Assistant Secretary to the Government of India (c. 1862-1876).
James Thomas Molesworth was an Indologist and linguist. His career included serving as a linguist for the Bombay Native Infantry in 1814 and for the Commissariat Department.

James Tod worked in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, and under Gyanchandra; he served in the East India Company (c. 1798-1823) and as Librarian of the Royal Asiatic Society (c. 1823-1835).
James W. Benson is an Indologist and linguist who held academic posts at Harvard University (attested 1999), the University of Oxford (attested 1999), and Wolfson College, Oxford (attested 2001).

James W. Heisig is a scholar of philosophy, religious studies, and Japanology. Educated at Divine Word, Loyola, Notre Dame, and Cambridge (PhD 1973), he was a longtime Permanent Research Fellow at Nanzan University and the Nanzan Institute (c. 1978-2014).
James Ward was a philosopher who studied at Fitzwilliam College and Trinity College, Cambridge (c. 1872-1875). He later held an academic post at the University of Cambridge from c. 1897 to 1925.
James Whitehill is a scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and philosophy. He founded the Columbia Zen Center and served as Professor of Religion at Stephens College (attested 2000).
